title: Reading a blood pressure
body: Blood pressure is written as two numbers, such as 120/80 mmHg. The top (systolic) is the pressure as the heart squeezes; the bottom (diastolic) is between beats. The WHO defines hypertension as 140/90 or higher on repeated readings. It usually has no symptoms.

title: Resting heart rate
body: A normal adult resting heart rate is about 60 to 100 beats per minute. Fit athletes can be in the 40s because each beat pumps more blood. A fast resting rate can come from fever, dehydration, anaemia, stress, caffeine or heart problems.

title: What blood is made of
body: Blood is about 55% plasma (water, salts, proteins, sugar) and 45% cells. Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin; white cells fight infection; platelets start clotting. Anaemia means too little haemoglobin, causing tiredness and breathlessness.

title: Blood groups
body: Red cells carry A, B, both or neither antigen (groups A, B, AB, O), plus Rh positive or negative. The wrong transfusion triggers a dangerous immune reaction. O negative red cells can be given to almost anyone in an emergency; AB positive patients can receive any group.

title: How vaccines work
body: A vaccine shows your immune system a harmless version or piece of a germ. It learns to recognise it and keeps memory cells, so a later real infection is fought off fast, often before you get sick. Vaccines have eliminated smallpox and nearly eliminated polio.

title: Viruses versus bacteria
body: Bacteria are living cells; many are harmless or helpful. Viruses are far smaller and can only multiply inside our cells. Antibiotics kill bacteria but do nothing to viruses, so they don't help colds or flu. Some viruses have antivirals, such as ART for HIV.

title: Malaria
body: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites spread by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Fever, chills and headache after travel to a malaria area need a rapid diagnostic test the same day. It is curable with artemisinin-based combination therapy, but severe malaria can kill within a day.

title: HIV and antiretroviral therapy
body: HIV attacks CD4 immune cells. Daily antiretroviral therapy (ART) stops the virus multiplying, lets the immune system recover and gives a near-normal life expectancy. A person whose viral load stays undetectable on ART does not pass HIV to sexual partners.
source_name: World Health Organization: HIV and AIDS

title: Tuberculosis is curable
body: TB is a bacterial infection spread through the air, usually affecting the lungs. Warning signs: a cough for over two weeks, fever, night sweats and weight loss. Standard treatment is a combination of antibiotics for about six months, and finishing the course prevents drug-resistant TB.

title: Cholera and oral rehydration
body: Cholera spreads through water or food contaminated with faeces and causes severe watery diarrhoea. Most patients can be saved with oral rehydration solution (ORS) given quickly. Safe water, sanitation and hand washing prevent outbreaks.

title: Type 2 diabetes
body: In type 2 diabetes the body stops responding well to insulin, so blood sugar stays high and slowly damages eyes, kidneys, nerves and blood vessels. Risk rises with excess weight and inactivity. Diet, exercise and medicines such as metformin control it.

title: Body mass index
body: BMI = weight in kg ÷ (height in m)². 18.5–24.9 counts as a healthy range for most adults, 25–29.9 overweight and 30+ obese. It is a quick screening tool, not a diagnosis: very muscular people score high, and waist size adds useful information.

title: Spot a stroke: FAST
body: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty: Time to get emergency help. A stroke is a blocked or burst blood vessel in the brain, and about two million brain cells die each minute it is untreated. Clot-busting treatment works only in the first few hours.

title: Heart attack warning signs
body: A heart attack is a blocked artery starving heart muscle of oxygen. Typical signs: crushing chest pain or pressure lasting minutes, spreading to the arm, jaw or back, with sweating, breathlessness or nausea. Women and diabetics may have milder symptoms. Get help immediately.

title: Hands-only CPR
body: If an adult collapses and is not breathing normally, call for help and push hard and fast in the centre of the chest: 5–6 cm deep, 100–120 times a minute, letting the chest rise fully. Use an AED as soon as one arrives. Doing something is far better than nothing.

title: Drug half-life
body: Half-life is the time for a drug's blood level to halve. After four to five half-lives it is mostly gone, and with regular doses it reaches a steady state in about the same time. That is why some medicines take days to work fully.

title: Antibiotic resistance
body: When antibiotics are overused or courses stopped early, surviving bacteria that resist the drug multiply. The WHO ranks antimicrobial resistance among the top global health threats. Use antibiotics only when prescribed and take the full course as directed.

title: Why sleep matters
body: During sleep the brain consolidates memories and clears waste products. Most adults need around 7 to 9 hours. Regular short sleep is linked to poorer concentration, weaker immunity, weight gain, high blood pressure and more accidents, including at the wheel.

title: Paracetamol has a limit
body: Paracetamol is safe at normal doses, but too much damages the liver, sometimes fatally, and symptoms can take a day to appear. For adults the usual maximum is 4 g in 24 hours. Many cold and flu remedies also contain paracetamol, so doses can add up by accident.

title: Randomised controlled trials
body: To test a treatment fairly, patients are randomly split into groups receiving the new treatment or a placebo or standard care. Double-blinding hides who gets what from both patients and doctors. Randomisation removes bias; blinding removes the effect of expectations.

title: Sensitivity and specificity
body: Sensitivity is the share of sick people a test correctly flags; specificity is the share of healthy people it correctly clears. When a disease is rare, even a 99% specific test produces many false positives, which is why positive screening results are confirmed.

title: The ECG
body: An electrocardiogram records the heart's electrical activity through skin electrodes. The P wave is the atria contracting, the QRS complex the ventricles, and the T wave their recovery. Irregular rhythms and heart attacks leave recognisable patterns.

title: Seeing inside the body
body: X-rays show bone well. CT combines many X-rays into 3D slices. MRI uses strong magnets and radio waves, with no ionising radiation, and shows soft tissue in detail. Ultrasound uses sound echoes, is cheap and safe, and is used in pregnancy.

title: Depression is treatable
body: Depression is more than sadness: low mood or loss of interest lasting at least two weeks, often with poor sleep, low energy and hopelessness. It is common and treatable with talking therapies, and sometimes medicine. Anyone thinking of self-harm should seek help urgently.

title: About 100,000 heartbeats a day
body: At around 70 beats per minute, your heart beats about 100,000 times a day and about 2.5 billion times in a lifetime, pumping roughly 5 litres of blood every minute at rest.

title: Penicillin was found by accident
body: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that mould growing on a forgotten bacterial culture had killed the bacteria around it. Mass production during the 1940s turned penicillin into the first widely used antibiotic, saving millions of lives.

title: Antibiotics and flu
body: Infection check.
explanation: Antibiotics only kill bacteria. Flu is caused by a virus; rest, fluids and sometimes antivirals help, and the flu vaccine prevents it.

title: High blood pressure
body: Cardiology check.
statement: A repeated reading of 140/90 mmHg counts as high blood pressure
explanation: The WHO defines hypertension as 140/90 mmHg or higher on repeated readings.

title: The universal donor
body: Blood check.
statement: O negative red cells can be given to almost anyone
explanation: O negative red cells carry no A, B or RhD antigens, so they are used in emergencies before the patient's group is known.

title: How malaria spreads
body: Infection check.
statement: Malaria spreads from person to person by coughing
explanation: Malaria parasites are carried by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Nets, repellents and indoor spraying prevent it.

title: Half-lives
body: Pharmacology check.
statement: After three half-lives, 12.5% of a drug remains
explanation: 100% → 50% → 25% → 12.5%. Each half-life halves what is left.
